claims.heading: ## Summary
claims.claim: **TL;DR:** With `EPOLLET` (edge-triggered, ET), once an event has been copied out to user space the kernel does not put the item back on the ready list; in the default level-triggered (LT) mode it does, so the next `epoll_wait` checks the file again ✅[^eventpoll]
claims.context: **TL;DR:** With `EPOLLET` (edge-triggered, ET), once an event has been copied out to user space the kernel does not put the item back on the ready list; in the default level-triggered (LT) mode it does, so the next `epoll_wait` checks the file again ✅[^eventpoll]. That is why, under ET, a partial read can leave data that the next `epoll_wait` does not report, and why the man page's suggested use is non-blocking file descriptors (fds) plus waiting for an event only after `read`/`write` returns `EAGAIN` ✅[^epoll7].

claims.heading: ## 1. Mental model
claims.claim: **The two modes, in the man page's words.** Edge-triggered mode "delivers events only when changes occur on the monitored file descriptor", that is, an event is generated upon each receipt of a chunk of data; level-triggered mode is the default (no `EPOLLET`), and then epoll "is simply a faster poll(2)" with the same semantics ✅[^epoll7]
claims.context: **The two modes, in the man page's words.** Edge-triggered mode "delivers events only when changes occur on the monitored file descriptor", that is, an event is generated upon each receipt of a chunk of data; level-triggered mode is the default (no `EPOLLET`), and then epoll "is simply a faster poll(2)" with the same semantics ✅[^epoll7].

claims.heading: ## 1. Mental model
claims.claim: **The two modes, in the kernel.** In v6.12 the difference is one branch in `ep_send_events`, after an event has been copied to user space: a level-triggered item is inserted back into the ready list "so that the next call to epoll_wait() will check again the events availability", and an `EPOLLET` item is not ✅[^eventpoll]
claims.context: **The two modes, in the kernel.** In v6.12 the difference is one branch in `ep_send_events`, after an event has been copied to user space: a level-triggered item is inserted back into the ready list "so that the next call to epoll_wait() will check again the events availability", and an `EPOLLET` item is not ✅[^eventpoll]. The rest of this doc follows from that branch: an ET item is reported again when something puts it back on the ready list, namely the file's wakeup callback, or an `EPOLL_CTL_ADD`/`EPOLL_CTL_MOD` that finds the file ready (§3).

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: While events are being transferred to user space, it chains the item on `ovflist` to be requeued later; otherwise, if the item is not already linked, it adds it to the tail of `rdllist`; then it wakes, if they have waiters, the `epoll_wait` wait queue (`ep->wq`) and the epoll file's own `->poll()` wait list ✅[^eventpoll]

While events are being transferred to user space, it chains the item on `ovflist` to be requeued later; otherwise, if the item is not already linked, it adds it to the tail of `rdllist`; then it wakes, if they have waiters, the `epoll_wait` wait queue (`ep->wq`) and the epoll file's own `->poll()` wait list ✅[^eventpoll].

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: Because an item that is already linked is not added again, several events that occur between two `epoll_wait` calls are combined, not reported separately ✅[^eventpoll][^epoll7]
claims.context: Because an item that is already linked is not added again, several events that occur between two `epoll_wait` calls are combined, not reported separately ✅[^eventpoll][^epoll7]. And because the callback runs only when the watched file wakes its wait queue, a file that does not wake it for new data produces no new ET event: §6.3 tells how pipes did exactly that from Linux 5.5 to a 2021 fix.

claims.claim: When nothing is available and the timeout is not zero (a zero timeout returns 0 before this point), `ep_poll` adds the calling thread to `ep->wq` with `__add_wait_queue_exclusive`; this path has no `EPOLLET` test ✅[^eventpoll]

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: `ep_send_events` starts with `ep_start_scan`, which moves the whole ready list to a private list, re-initializes `rdllist` to empty, and sets `ovflist` to NULL so that events happening during the copy are not lost ✅[^eventpoll]

claims.heading: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions
claims.claim: epoll(7) describes `EPOLLWAKEUP` keeping the system awake from the moment the event is queued, with no condition ✅[^epoll7]
claims.context: - *Does `EPOLLWAKEUP` apply together with `EPOLLET`?* ⚠️ unverified. epoll(7) describes `EPOLLWAKEUP` keeping the system awake from the moment the event is queued, with no condition ✅[^epoll7]; epoll_ctl(2) says it applies only if `EPOLLONESHOT` and `EPOLLET` are clear and the process has `CAP_BLOCK_SUSPEND` ✅[^epollctl]. In the v6.12 source, the registration check `ep_take_care_of_epollwakeup` clears `EPOLLWAKEUP` only when the caller lacks `CAP_BLOCK_SUSPEND` (or the kernel has no `CONFIG_PM_SLEEP`), with no `EPOLLET` test ✅[^eventpoll]. When `ep_send_events` delivers an item, it relaxes the item's wakeup source (`__pm_relax(ws)`) and calls `ep_pm_stay_awake(epi)` again only in the level-triggered branch, while `ep_poll_callback` calls `ep_pm_stay_awake_rcu(epi)` whenever it queues an item, with no `EPOLLET` test ✅[^eventpoll]. So for an `EPOLLET` item nothing is held after `epoll_wait` returns it, which matches epoll_ctl(2)'s condition for the time the event is being processed, but the time it is pending is not conditioned on `EPOLLET`. All three are Rank 1; the part after `epoll_wait` returns is settled by the code, the pending part stays open.

claims.context: - *Does `EPOLLWAKEUP` apply together with `EPOLLET`?* ⚠️ unverified. epoll(7) describes `EPOLLWAKEUP` keeping the system awake from the moment the event is queued, with no condition ✅[^epoll7]; epoll_ctl(2) says it applies only if `EPOLLONESHOT` and `EPOLLET` are clear and the process has `CAP_BLOCK_SUSPEND` ✅[^epollctl]. In the v6.12 source, the registration check `ep_take_care_of_epollwakeup` clears `EPOLLWAKEUP` only when the caller lacks `CAP_BLOCK_SUSPEND` (or the kernel has no `CONFIG_PM_SLEEP`), with no `EPOLLET` test ✅[^eventpoll]. When `ep_send_events` delivers an item, it relaxes the item's wakeup source (`__pm_relax(ws)`) and calls `ep_pm_stay_awake(epi)` again only in the level-triggered branch, while `ep_poll_callback` calls `ep_pm_stay_awake_rcu(epi)` whenever it queues an item, with no `EPOLLET` test ✅[^eventpoll]. So for an `EPOLLET` item nothing is held after `epoll_wait` returns it, which matches epoll_ctl(2)'s condition for the time the event is being processed, but the time it is pending is not conditioned on `EPOLLET`. All three are Rank 1; the part after `epoll_wait` returns is settled by the code, the pending part stays open.

claims.heading: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions
claims.claim: In 2003 Eric Varsanyi reported that under edge-triggered epoll, a client that writes data and then shuts down its write side gives the server a single `EPOLLIN` for both, with no way to tell that EOF also occurred, and proposed a `POLLRDHUP` event ✅[^lkml2003]
claims.context: In 2003 Eric Varsanyi reported that under edge-triggered epoll, a client that writes data and then shuts down its write side gives the server a single `EPOLLIN` for both, with no way to tell that EOF also occurred, and proposed a `POLLRDHUP` event ✅[^lkml2003]. `EPOLLRDHUP` exists since Linux 2.6.17 (§3.8), and nginx's `pending_eof` comes from it (§5.3).
